records.title: Treatment outcomes and influencing factors of older patients with pulmonary tuberculosis complicated with diabetes mellitus in China, 2018–2024
records.abstract: The comorbidity of pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) and diabetes mellitus (DM) is rising among adults aged ≥ 65 years in China. DM comorbidity significantly worsens PTB treatment outcomes. Population-based evidence specific to older Chinese PTB-DM patients remains scarce. This retrospective cohort study aimed to identify independent risk factors for adverse treatment outcomes in older Chinese PTB-DM patients.  Data were from the National Tuberculosis Information Management System (2018–2024). Kaplan–Meier analysis was performed to estimate overall event-free survival. Fine–Gray competing risks regression models were used to identify independent factors associated with each adverse outcome subtype, accounting for competing events.  Among 56,682 eligible patients, the median follow-up duration was 6.965 months, and the rate of adverse anti-tuberculosis treatment outcomes was 11.08%. Irregular treatment adherence ( aHR = 12.783, 95%CI : 12.008–13.607), male sex ( aHR = 1.246, 95%CI : 1.176–1.319), increased age ( aHR = 1.345–2.459), retreatment ( aHR = 1.112, 95%CI : 1.031–1.199), positive etiological test  ( aHR = 1.338, 95%CI : 1.259–1.421), comorbidities other than diabetes ( aHR = 1.234, 95%CI : 1.154–1.320), and non-guideline-concordant regimens, ( aHR = 1.096, 95%CI : 1.025–1.171) were independent risk factors for adverse treatment outcomes.  Adverse treatment outcomes in older adults with PTB-DM are driven by a range of demographic, clinical and adherence-related factors, with irregular medication adherence being the most robust predictor. These risk factors differ across adverse outcome subtypes.

records.title: New horizons in adaptive capacity and heat-related health in older people: integrating frailty, energy insecurity and social resources
records.abstract: Extreme heat is a major environmental threat to healthy ageing, with older people experiencing the highest rates of heat-related morbidity and mortality. Although age-related physiological changes, multimorbidity and frailty remain key determinants of heat susceptibility, climate change, social inequalities and energy insecurity are reshaping the conditions in which older people experience and respond to thermal stress. This narrative New Horizons review integrates evidence identified through a structured, non-systematic search of peer-reviewed literature and relevant institutional reports across geriatric medicine, environmental health and climate science. It examines how frailty, intrinsic capacity, housing, energy affordability and social frailty influence the ability of older people to recognise risk, access protection and respond effectively to extreme heat. Particular attention is given to energy insecurity and summer cooling poverty, through which limited access to affordable household energy may undermine resilience. Ageing models primarily characterise individual vulnerability and functioning within the environment, whereas climate vulnerability models organise risk around exposure, sensitivity and adaptation; we use adaptive capacity to connect these perspectives by asking whether personal and contextual resources can be mobilised for protection. It may provide a conceptual basis for developing and subsequently validating a heat-adapted comprehensive geriatric assessment and for informing targeted prevention and climate adaptation policies for ageing populations.

records.title: Clinical characteristics and establishment of clinical prediction model for traumatic cholecystitis in older patients with hip fracture: a retrospective machine learning models and SHAP value-based interpretation model
records.abstract: Traumatic cholecystitis after hip fracture is rare, but its prognosis is poor. However, studies that explore the risk factors for traumatic cholecystitis in older patients with hip fractures and establish effective predictive models were limited. Therefore, our study focused on the following three questions: (1)What were the characteristics of traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients? (2) What were the risk factors for traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients? (3) What was the best model for predicting traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients and analyze it globally and locally interpretatively using SHAP values?  We retrospectively collected all clinical parameters of older hip fracture patients admitted to the Third Hospital of Hebei Medical University from January 2018 to December 2022. We developed five machine learning models for traumatic cholecystitis, which included logistic regression model(LR), random forest model(RF), lightGBM, XGBoost and KNN. We evaluate the predictive performance and clinical applicability of the LR model using the area under the ROC curve, calibration curve, and clinical decision curve. We evaluated the machine learning models by calculating AUC-ROC, PR-AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 score. SHAP values were used to interpret the models, enhancing clinicians’ understanding and application of the models.  This study included 2376 patients, with an incidence rate of traumatic cholecystitis of 1.3% (30/2376). Independent risk factors for traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients included the C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR), history of biliary disease, haemoglobin (HB), albumin, hypokalaemia, and CRP. RF showed the highest PR-AUC (0.940, 95% CI: 0.835–0.997) among the five models. The ROC-AUC for the five models were 0.999(95% CI: 0.998,1.000) (RF), 0.741(95% CI: 0.649,0.839) (XGBoost), 0.852(95% CI: 0.785,0.915) (LR), 0.971(95% CI: 0.955,0.984) (LightGBM), and 0.980(95% CI: 0.975,0.985) (KNN), with sensitivities ranging from 26.7% (LR) to 100% (RF). The accuracy of these models ranged from 91.8%% (LightGBM) to 99.7% (RF). The random forest model performed the best. Discussion Among the five machine learning models, the random forest model showed the best discriminative performance in the present dataset, but this exploratory finding may overestimate its true predictive capability because of the small number of positive cases and lack of external validation. SHAP values were used to improve model interpretability. In the absence of large-scale prospective validation, this random forest algorithm can serve as an auxiliary perioperative comprehensive risk stratification tool, helping clinicians identify potential high-risk older patients as early as possible and implement closer monitoring of abdominal signs.

records.title: Comparison of the Clinical Frailty Scale and the FRAIL Scale for predicting short-term outcomes in older adults hospitalized with infectious diseases: a multicentre prospective study
records.abstract: Frailty is a major determinant of adverse health outcomes in older adults, yet evidence comparing commonly used frailty instruments in patients hospitalized with infectious diseases is limited. We aimed to compare the prognostic performance of the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and the FRAIL Scale for predicting short-term outcomes in older adults admitted to infectious diseases departments.  This prospective multicentre observational cohort study included adults aged ≥ 65 years hospitalized in infectious diseases departments across 16 hospitals in Türkiye. Frailty was rated at enrolment, during acute illness, using the CFS (frail: ≥5) and the FRAIL Scale (frail: ≥3). The primary outcome was a composite poor 28-day outcome, defined by day-28 status as being in the intensive care unit, ongoing general-ward hospitalization, or death within 28 days. Separate multivariable logistic regression models using the same covariates and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to compare the two instruments.  Among 151 older adults, 102 (67.5%) were classified as frail by the FRAIL Scale and 87 (57.6%) by the CFS. Poor 28-day outcome occurred in 18 patients (11.9%). It was more frequent among CFS-defined frail than non-frail patients (18.4% vs. 3.1%, p = 0.004), whereas the difference by FRAIL classification was not statistically significant (15.7% vs. 4.1%, p = 0.058). After adjustment for age, sex, and polypharmacy, CFS-defined frailty was associated with higher odds of poor 28-day outcome (adjusted OR 5.99, 95% CI 1.26–28.42; p = 0.024), whereas FRAIL-defined frailty was not significantly associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 3.63, 95% CI 0.76–17.41; p = 0.107). The CFS showed an AUC of 0.823 (95% CI 0.702–0.944), compared with 0.696 (95% CI 0.579–0.813) for the FRAIL Scale; the difference between the AUCs was statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.034).  In this cohort, CFS ratings obtained during acute hospitalization showed higher discrimination for poor 28-day outcome than the FRAIL Scale and remained associated with the outcome after adjustment for age, sex, and polypharmacy. Given the limited number of events and assessment during acute illness rather than for pre-illness status, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, may not apply directly to standard pre-illness CFS assessment, and require validation in larger cohorts.

records.title: Social Engagement and Cognitive Function Among Chinese Older Adults During the COVID-19 Outbreak: Gender and Urban–Rural Disparities
records.abstract: This study examines the association between reduced social engagement and cognitive function among older adults in China during the COVID-19 pandemic with a focus on gender and urban–rural differences.  Using China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study data, we used OLS regression to assess changes in cognitive function before and during the pandemic and their associations with changes in physical and cognitively stimulating activities.  Cognitive function declined across social groups, with the largest decline among urban women. Moderate physical activity was not associated with less cognitive function, whereas decreased engagement in cognitively stimulating activities was associated with greater decline.  Forms of social engagement were associated with cognitive function of older adults in distinct ways, underscoring the need for a nuanced rather than uniform interpretation. The observed differences in cognitive function by subgroups suggest a need for targeted interventions to support older populations in the post-pandemic context.

records.title: Exploring Quality of Life Through Residents’ Voice in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of a Montessori-Based Person-Centered Model of Care
records.abstract: Person-centered care (PCC) is the gold standard for improving the quality of life (QoL) of people living with dementia. The Montessori method represents a practical model for implementing PCC in Nursing Homes (NHs). To date, no study has documented how residents describe their QoL in NHs implementing this method using a self-report approach consistent with PCC principles. This study explores residents’ perceptions of their QoL, as well as how they relate it to the care model, using a qualitative self-assessment tool. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-nine residents from two NHs with high levels of Montessori implementation assessed using a validated tool. All interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three interconnected themes emerged. The first examines the components of QoL that matter most to residents. The second explores how the care model influences these determinants. Finally, the third describes residents’ self-assessment of QoL shaped by individual factors. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the Montessori method as a comprehensive PCC model from residents’ perspectives and deepens knowledge of the extent to which it can shape their QoL. These findings also provide practical and methodological insights for evaluating QoL and guiding care models promoting QoL.

records.title: Perceptions, Knowledge, and Adaptive actions in Response to Climate Events: A Scoping Review of Climate Health Literacy among Community Dwelling Older Adults
records.abstract: and  Extreme climate events can threaten older adults’ health. The purpose of this study was to summarize existing literature on older adults’ climate health literacy, defined as their ability to find and access, understand, and act upon information related to climate-related health threats. Research Design and  A scoping review was conducted in the bibliographic databases Embase, Medline and Scopus and grey literature sources Cornell Initiative for Research on Climate and Aging and Climate Change and Human Health Literature portals with searches updated January 2026. English language studies of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older were included if they reported at least one aspect of climate health literacy. Quantitative data were reported as median percentages, and qualitative themes were categorized.  Fifty-nine studies, including 22,992 records for 20,296 unique participants, were included. Most recognized the health risks of extreme climate events but did not identify personal vulnerability. Television was the most cited source of information and hydration, clothing and environment modification, and activity adjustment were the most utilized adaptive actions. Barriers to adaptive actions included financial constraints, limited mobility and lack of supports. The effectiveness of studied interventions was mixed, influenced by intervention type and study design.  Despite access to information and awareness of climate-related health threats, gaps remain in personal risk perception and translation of knowledge into actions. Improving climate health literacy among older adults requires public health messaging, engagement of trustworthy authorities, and interventions addressing social and structural barriers.

records.title: Adaptive driving, not unsafe: Older drivers’ compensatory strategies and lower simulated crash risk
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The global aging population has led to an increasing number of older active drivers. While age-related physical and cognitive changes are associated with increased crash risk, specific on-road adaptations and safety outcomes of older drivers remain unclear. This study examined distinct driving characteristics, personality traits, and cognitive processes related to decision-making among middle-aged and older drivers in a simulated driving environment.  We assessed driving performance in a high-fidelity motorcycle simulator across drivers in three age groups: middle-aged (30-54; n = 40), aged 65–74 (n = 34), and aged 75 + (75-86; n = 29). Comparative analysis focused on speed regulation, braking behavior, control stability, and accident rates. Additionally, questionnaire measures and a computerized decision-making task were employed to assess risk perception and risky decision-making.  Compared to the middle-aged group, both older groups demonstrated a significantly more conservative driving profile: lower mean speeds, fewer speeding violations, longer braking maneuvers, reduced variation in throttle control, and a lower incidence of simulated accidents. Drivers aged 75+ also reported higher perceived risk in driving scenarios and displayed diminished discrimination between risk and non-risk situations in a braking decision task. Mediation analyses showed that steering variance in the simulator and self-reported health/safety risk-taking significantly mediated the relationship between age group and number of accidents. Discussion The findings indicate that older drivers adopt proactive compensatory strategies that could result in fewer simulated accidents. These findings challenge a purely deficit-oriented perspective on older driver safety, underscoring the critical role of behavioral adaptation and strategic self-regulation in maintaining safe mobility.

records.title: Weekly community mobility patterns among older adults in a Brazilian city: a GPS-based study
records.abstract: Active community mobility is critical for preserving physical health, autonomy, and functional capacity in older adults. However, in Latin America,  assessments using Global Positioning System (GPS) data remain scarce, hindering the development of targeted, evidence-based strategies for healthy aging.  To characterize weekly mobility patterns and analyze variations in active travel based on sociodemographic, health, and environmental factors among older adults in a Brazilian urban setting.  This cross-sectional study involved 276 community-dwelling individuals (≥ 60 years) in Florianópolis, Brazil. Participants wore a GPS device for seven consecutive days to objectively record all trips and travel modes. Data were integrated with household interview  and neighborhood-level census data (walkability and income).  Participants averaged 23.3 trips per week, with 71.7% classified as active (primarily walking). Despite this high frequency, only 9.8% met the ≥ 150 min/week physical activity threshold through transportation alone. Active travel significantly differed by education level and nutritional status ( p  While older adults engage frequently in active travel, the volume is often insufficient to meet global physical activity recommendations.  GPS data offer crucial insights for designing age-friendly urban policies and public health interventions tailored to middle-income contexts. Clinical Trial Registration Not applicable. records.title: Daily patterns and prevalence of behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia in Swedish nursing homes
records.abstract: Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are among the principal observable expressions of psychological distress and unmet need in nursing home residents who can no longer reliably verbalize internal experiences, and recognizing their day-to-day variation underpins timely, person-centered care. Yet BPSD fluctuate across days, shifts, and contexts, while established instruments such as the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Nursing Home version (NPI-NH) assess them retrospectively over the preceding weeks or months. This mismatch leaves basic descriptive questions about the day-to-day symptom landscape in routine care unanswered. This study describes the prevalence, severity, co-occurrence, between-unit variation, and shift and weekday patterns of BPSD documented through structured daily registrations in nursing home care.  Descriptive longitudinal observational study of 230 individuals with dementia in six nursing homes across six Swedish municipalities, followed for a median observation period of 270 days (interquartile range 120 to 446). Care staff used a digital tool to rate the severity (0–3) of twelve common BPSD, adapted from the NPI-NH, at the end of every work shift, yielding over one million symptom registrations. Analyses were descriptive and person-weighted, giving each individual equal weight regardless of observation length.  Cumulative symptom prevalence (at any point during observation) ranged from 90% (agitation) to 70% (euphoria). Each symptom’s mean daily prevalence was much lower (4–18%), and symptoms were predominantly of low severity. At least one symptom was recorded on a median of 43.5% of registered days, varying widely between individuals. Clinically related symptoms tended to occur together, consistent with established NPI-NH domain structures, and the mean number of symptoms per day varied more than twofold across the six units. Symptoms were most frequent on evening shifts and least frequent at night, except sleep disturbances, with little variation across weekdays. Just under half of all possible shift registrations were completed.  Daily registrations describe an intermittent and heterogeneous symptom landscape at a resolution that periodic assessments are not designed to provide. These findings provide an empirical baseline for future multilevel analyses and support BPSD monitoring that covers both individual symptoms and the daily number of symptoms in nursing homes. records.title: Living Alone With Dementia: Managing Without Informal Support to Contact and Navigate Services
records.abstract: Purpose: People with dementia can and do live successfully on their own, but there are additional challenges for people living alone without informal support. This paper reports findings of the first study in the UK to examine needs and experiences of, and services for, people with dementia who live alone without informal support. Method: The study involved a service audit of 13 local authority commissioners in two English regions, interviews with 22 people with dementia who live alone without informal carers, and case studies of four services supporting this group. Findings: Awareness of this population among commissioners was limited. There were very few services which explicitly supported this group, and some mainstream services excluded people without carers. None of the local authorities collected data on numbers of people with dementia living alone, or those without informal support, in their area. Some participants with dementia had contacted social care, but this had not always resulted in appropriate support, and people reported problematic interactions with staff, assumptions that friends would provide care, and support not being available at the right time. Self-funders were left with little support. People with dementia were resourceful, using general services, technology, and other tactics, including cleaners, meal delivery, community taxis, and automatic reminders to organise their lives. However, as many of these additional services have a cost attached, there is potential to exacerbate existing inequalities. Participants wanted more support, particularly with finances and administrative tasks. Services can help this group with supported handovers, allowing self-referral back into a service, and keeping case files open. : Both the number of people with dementia, and the number of people ageing without children, are rising, and it will therefore become increasingly important to facilitate effective support for people with dementia to live independently without informal support.

records.title: Paramedics’ experiences of using the clinical frailty scale in prehospital care: a qualitative study
records.abstract: The demographic shift toward an ageing population has increased focus on frailty. Frailty has become increasingly recognized as a critical factor in clinical decision-making and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) has gained widespread use across healthcare settings. This study explores paramedics’ experiences using CFS for older patients.  This study uses a qualitative research design and incorporates semi-structured interviews to explore paramedics’ experience of the feasibility and practical application of CFS in prehospital care. The study is part of a larger project on the use of CFS for older patients (≥ 65 years) in prehospital care in the North Denmark Region. During the study period 432 of 2 084 patients (21%) had a documented CFS score. CFS scores spanned all nine categories of the scale. The study is inspired from hermeneutic philosophy and frailty assessment theory. Individual face-to-face semi-structured interviews were conducted, and data was analysed using thematic analysis, inspired by Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework.  A total of eleven paramedics participated in the interviews (ten men and one woman). The median age was 38 years, and participants had a median of 11 years of experience in the prehospital setting. Three main themes emerged: (1) Older patients – complexity and clinical assessment (2) Making CFS work in the prehospital practice (3) CFS as a shared language in cross-sector collaboration. Older patients were perceived as a complex and habitually ill population requiring an adapted clinical mindset. Distinction between acute illness and frailty was described as challenging in the prehospital setting. CFS was considered to serve as a bridge between sectors and professional discipline.  CFS was generally perceived as relevant and as a tool that can support continuity of care and create a shared language around frailty. The findings highlight the importance of paramedics understanding the purpose and application of CFS and how the assessment may contribute to patient care across sectors. These considerations may be relevant when supporting the use of CFS in routine prehospital practice. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Telemonitoring Adoption Among Older Adults: Sequential Mixed Methods Study of Message Framing and Structural Influence
records.abstract: Telemonitoring offers solutions for remote health management among older adults; yet, acceptance varies based on individual perceptions and presentation strategies.  This 2-phased sequential mixed  study examines the role of message framing on telemonitoring adoption among low-income older adults.  Phase 1 involved in-depth interviews with 17 older adults, identifying key facilitators (accessibility, affordability, and health benefits) and barriers (preference for in-person consultations, technological limitations, and information processing difficulties) of telemonitoring. Building on these insights, phase 2 used an experimental study with 120 participants assessing message framing effects (episodic vs thematic) and modalities (video vs photo-text) on telemonitoring adoption.  Episodic framing did not produce a significant main effect on attitudes toward telemonitoring; however, its effect was moderated by external locus of control (LOC), with episodic framing associated with more positive attitudes among participants lower in external LOC, and thematic framing more favorable among those higher in external LOC.  Convenience, cost, and health benefits emerged as key adoption drivers, while traditional consultation preferences and cognitive processing challenges posed barriers. Theoretical and practical implications were discussed.

records.title: I Did It My Way Theatre: Research and Live Theatre as Applied to the Transition of Relocating Older Adults
records.abstract: Relocation is an option for older adults who leave their home to improve their emotional well-being, physical health, and safety. Moves can enhance agency or foster a loss of empowerment. We explored older adults’ transition experiences from a community setting to a retirement community and created messaging to help with experiences of older adults and their self-identified family or friend caregivers. We conducted 30 telephone interviews and analyzed relocation experiences, which informed I Did It My Way Theatre. The theatrical presentation was performed for over 100 older adult residents and caregivers. Our goal was to ease the transition experiences by disseminating findings to those involved in similar relocation situations. Attendees completed a post-performance questionnaire asking how the play helped them understand relocation and held table discussions concerning production themes. Follow-up interviews with 11 participants revealed that the play delivered hard messages in an impactful way.

records.title: Dementia Knowledge Among Older Asian Americans: Roles of Digital Literacy, Planning Attitudes, and Sociocultural Contexts
records.abstract: Knowledge of dementia facilitates early detection, care planning, and stigma reduction, yet less is known about dementia knowledge among Asian American populations. This study examined correlates of dementia knowledge among 505 Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese Americans aged 50 and older residing in Central Florida. Dementia knowledge was assessed using the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale with four subscales. Linear regression analyses examined associations of dementia knowledge with sociodemographic, immigration, social, digital and information, and dementia experiences and attitudinal factors. Participants demonstrated low overall dementia knowledge. Digital literacy was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and all subscales except communication and behavior. Limited English proficiency was negatively associated with knowledge in the causes and characteristics subscale. The perceived importance of dementia planning was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and three subscales. Subscale-specific findings should be interpreted cautiously because of varying subscale reliability, particularly for communication and behavior.

records.title: Third Places, Walkable Access, and Neighborhood Satisfaction Among Older Adults
records.abstract: Neighborhood satisfaction is a key indicator of well-being and community quality of life, yet its relationship with third place engagement remains underexplored.  This study examines how third place engagement, access, and perceived built environments relate to physical livability, social connectedness, and overall neighborhood satisfaction among older adults.  Survey data were collected from 515 adults aged 65 and older in the Orlando area, and separate Ordinary Least Squares regression models were used.  The  indicate that neighborhood satisfaction is multidimensional, with shared yet distinct correlates across domains. Third place engagement and walkable access were consistently associated with all three outcomes. Socially oriented third place use was more closely tied to social connectedness, while built environment quality aligned with physical livability. Overall satisfaction reflected both domains, highlighting the value of viewing neighborhood satisfaction as related but distinct constructs shaped by functional and social experiences among older adults.

records.title: The relationship between empathic tendency and aged discrimination attitudes of nurses
records.abstract: Aim This study aimed to examine the relationship between nurses’ empathic tendencies and their attitudes toward age discrimination.  This is a cross-sectional correlational study included a sample of 305 nurses reached through the snowball sampling method. Data were collected online between April and May 2023 using a Personal Information Form, the Empathic Tendency Scale (ETS), and the Ageism Attitude Scale (AAS). The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and linear regression analysis. This study report followed the STROBE reporting guidelines.  The majority of nurses were female, with a mean age of 34.02 ± 8.20 years. Most participants held a bachelor’s degree, and while over half reported a preference for caring for older patients, the majority experienced difficulties in geriatric care. Additionally, more than half had not received training related to the care of older adults. The mean total score of the ETS was 68.453 ± 5.836, while the mean total score of the AAS was 68.797 ± 6.736. A significant relationship was found between the total score of the ETS and both the total score of the AAS and the positive discrimination toward older adults subdimension ( r = 0.201, p r = 0.239, p p p  The findings indicate a positive and significant association between nurses’ empathic tendencies and their attitudes toward age discrimination. Although the strength of this association was weak, higher empathic tendency was associated with more positive attitudes toward older adults. These findings suggest that empathic tendency may be one of several factors associated with nurses’ attitudes toward age discrimination.

records.title: Content Analysis of Free Online Information and Support Available to Young Dementia Carers Across Europe
records.abstract: The aim of this study was to gain insight into young dementia carer-specific content provided on the websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations in seven European countries including: the UK, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Portugal, Ireland and Sweden. Research questions were: 1). What types of young dementia carer-specific content are available on national websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations across Europe? and 2). How does the content address the complex impact that dementia can have on young dementia carers? The identification of websites was informed by the contextual characteristics of each country in relation to dementia and young carers support and services. A standard protocol describing the website inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction and content analysis using a categorical coding framework was followed. Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize data within and across countries. A total of 312 organizations with active websites meeting the eligibility criteria across countries were identified, and their websites reviewed. Content relevant to young dementia carers was identified in 28% (n = 86) of the websites, with uneven availability of resources across Europe and very limited resources in some countries. Most contents addressed five categories: Diagnosis & symptoms, Uncertainty & family distress, Changes in roles, Stigma & isolation and Identifying need for support. A lack of tailored resources to support young dementia carers was identified, particularly in relation to two categories: Grief & loss and Education & life planning. Only a minority of websites included young dementia carer-specific content. These websites primarily focused on general support needs and explanations of dementia, while key areas such as guidance on school, career, and life planning remain underdeveloped. records.title: Disrupted Activities and Caregivers' Resilience and Positive Affect
records.abstract: and  Caregiving for older adults imposes substantial physical and emotional costs, yet less attention has been paid to how disruptions in personally valued activities and caregiver–care recipient relationship quality relate to caregivers’ psychological well-being over time. Drawing on the activity restriction model and conservation of resource theory, this longitudinal study examined how within-person changes in disrupted valued activities (DVA) and negative relationship quality (NRQ) influence caregivers’ resilience and positive affect. Research Design and  Data came from three waves of the National Study of Caregiving, linked to the National Health and Aging Trends Study. The analytic sample included 2,415 caregivers who provided 3,441 caregiver-wave observations, nested within 1,559 care recipients. Three-level linear mixed models decomposed DVA and NRQ into between-person and within-person components and adjusted for caregiver characteristics, care-recipient dementia status, and activities of daily living (ADL) limitations.  Resilience and positive affect showed substantial variation between-person and within-person. Higher average and higher-than-usual DVA were each associated with lower positive affect and resilience. Higher average NRQ was associated with lower positive affect and resilience, whereas higher-than-usual NRQ was associated with lower positive affect but not resilience. Care-recipient dementia status and ADL limitations were not associated with either outcome once caregiver characteristics were considered.  DVA and NRQ appear to be distinct sources of resource loss, independently linked to lower caregiver well-being across and within caregivers over time. Interventions may be effective by targeting either the maintenance of meaningful activities or improvements in relationship quality.

records.title: Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy for Older Persons With Dementia: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Spirituality is a core component of person-centred dementia care, yet spiritual needs may be under-recognised as cognition and communication decline. Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy (SRT) is a structured intervention that emphasises meaning-making and existential reflection rather than autobiographical recall alone. We examined the clinical outcomes and implementation characteristics of SRT in older adults with dementia.  A scoping review was conducted using Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Electronic databases (Cochrane, EMBASE, MEDLINE, PubMed and PsycINFO) were searched from inception to 26 December 2025, supplemented by grey literature and reference screening. Eligible English-language quantitative and qualitative studies evaluating SRT in adults aged ≥65 years with dementia were included. Data were synthesised descriptively.  Four studies met inclusion criteria (2 qualitative, 1 randomized controlled trial, 1 prospective cohort study). SRT was associated with improvements in spiritual well-being, life meaning and hope. Psychological outcomes suggested increased life satisfaction and reduced depressive symptoms. Qualitative findings indicated enhanced social connectedness in residential care settings. Evidence for cognitive benefit was inconsistent and clinically modest, and functional outcomes were rarely assessed. Reporting of intervention delivery and implementation processes was variable.  SRT may improve meaning-related and depressive symptoms in persons with dementia, however extant evidence is limited and methodologically heterogenous. Future research prioritizing standardised outcomes, longer follow-up and formal implementation evaluation are needed before broader integration into routine psychogeriatric practice.

records.title: Epigenetic aging in people with HIV across the life course: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Epigenetic aging algorithms are emerging tools for understanding the biological effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A growing body of literature has applied DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks in people living with HIV (PWH) across the life course, examining epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) in relation to HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy (ART), comorbidities, and clinical biomarkers (e.g., viral load, CD4 T-cell counts). This systematic review (Prospero: CRD420251126874) summarizes and synthesizes the current evidence on epigenetic aging in PWH across the life course and identifies critical knowledge gaps for future research. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Medline through June 26, 2026. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and assessed studies for risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We created a narrative synthesis of  and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA. Fifty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. More than half (n = 33) examined EAA in PWH compared to an uninfected control population. We identified heterogeneity in study populations and design, biospecimens profiled, platforms used for DNA methylation analysis, and epigenetic clocks employed. Only 6 studies included participants younger than 18 years and no studies focused exclusively on individuals over 65 years. Only 10 studies examined longitudinal changes in EAA. Thirty-seven papers evaluated associations between EAA and comorbidities. A meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA across 14 studies found a mean difference of 3.41 years (95%CI 2.22, 4.60) in PWH relative to controls. Current evidence supports accelerated EAA among PWH but highlights substantial methodological heterogeneity and important knowledge gaps. Longitudinal studies of EAA in PWH are needed in populations under 18 and over 65, to clarify the effects of ART, clinical biomarkers, and age-related comorbidities, and determine the clinical utility of epigenetic aging biomarkers.

records.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
records.abstract: Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships.  This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender.  A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI.  DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116).  DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.

records.title: Development and Evaluation of a Transportation Planning e-Tool for Older Adults: Co-Design Study
records.abstract: Older adults often face challenges using digital transportation planning tools to engage in meaningful activities. In Sherbrooke, a Canadian city located in the province of Québec, hilly terrain, bus-based mobility, and varied digital literacy among older adults highlight the need for accessible transportation planning technologies. Despite the growing demand for accessible and inclusive technologies, interfaces are often not tailored to the specific needs and preferences of older adults, making them difficult to use. Addressing this gap is essential to support the mobility and social participation of older adults in their communities.  This study aimed to enhance older adults’ experience with a transportation planning e-tool—called Mobilainés—by co-designing its interface and evaluating its usability and user experience in line with their needs and preferences.  Using a participatory design approach, the study encompassed both development and evaluation phases, integrating qualitative and quantitative . In the development phase, heuristic evaluation, along with the Mobilaînés mock-up, was performed to identify the percentage of compatibility with age-friendly usability design principles and guidelines. Fourteen co-design workshops with the steering committee and research team informed persona development and core functionalities, while 3 workshops with older adults refined the mock-ups. For the evaluation phase, 2 laboratory usability tests (simulated context) and 1 in-field test (real-world context) were conducted with 5, 7, and 4 older adults, respectively. Data were collected using a combination of  performance metrics recorded in real time by a computer and subjective user feedback, gathered using the System Usability Scale, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology questionnaires, and focus group discussions. For the in-field testing, user experience data were obtained via the User Experience Questionnaire and semistructured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative data were analyzed thematically.  The participatory design and iterative evaluation process identified key design decisions for age-friendly transportation planning, including step-by-step navigation, simplified task flow, clear feedback, visual clarity, and personalization. In the final laboratory usability test, the Mobilaînés e-tool showed 84% compatibility with age-friendly guidelines, a 97% task completion rate, and System Usability Scale and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology scores corresponding to very good usability. In-field User Experience Questionnaire  and interviews suggested that participants perceived the e-tool as reliable, easy to use, and accurate, despite the lack of real-time data.  Participatory design and iterative usability testing revealed that older adults’ experience with Mobilainés transportation planning e-tools is improved. These design learnings contributed to improved usability and confidence in real-world travel planning, offering practical guidance for the development of age-friendly digital transportation tools. Future research should explore collaborative and technological strategies to support its adoption and sustained use, particularly among older adults with limited digital literacy.

records.title: The rigor in qualitative research framework: A practical guide to evaluating qualitative studies
records.abstract: Qualitative research is central to understanding aging-related experiences, yet expectations for rigor are often unclear and inconsistently applied across studies. Here, we introduce the Rigor in Qualitative Research Framework, developed through a structured review of qualitative quality frameworks and reporting guidance and application to qualitative articles published in Innovation in Aging. We identified ten domains of qualitative rigor that reflect core areas across qualitative approaches: methodological coherence, relevance and contribution, contextual sensitivity and transferability, researcher reflexivity and positioning, participant/data-item selection and composition, ethical and relational integrity, data generation quality and richness, analytic rigor and transparency, interpretive credibility and evidence linkage, and reporting clarity, coherence, and usability. We then examined how these domains are described and operationalized in 39 published qualitative studies from 2020-2025 in Innovation in Aging, identifying exemplars in how rigor is enacted in practice. Findings suggest that existing frameworks provide broad coverage of key domains but differ in scope, emphasis, and level of guidance; qualitative studies thus vary in how clearly and consistently these domains are articulated. In response, our proposed framework integrates these domains into a structure supporting both evaluation and application, while remaining flexible to different epistemological and methodological traditions. The Rigor in Qualitative Research Framework is intended to guide study design, analysis, and reporting, and to support more consistent evaluation during peer review, providing a practical reference point for qualitative research across applied health and gerontology.

records.title: Social Vulnerability and Suicidal Ideation in Nursing Home Residents: The Mediating Role of Meaning in Life
records.abstract: and  Suicidal ideation (SI) in nursing homes remains underexplored. This study examined whether meaning in life mediates associations between social vulnerability, perceived burdensomeness, and SI. Research Design and  This is a cross-sectional study with 231 residents from Valencian Community, Spain, aged 60 years or older with preserved or mildly impaired cognitive functioning. Structural equation modeling tested direct and indirect associations.  Lower meaning in life was associated with higher SI. Perceived burdensomeness and low social support were not directly associated with SI but were indirectly associated through reduced meaning in life, explaining 42.8% of its variance. Loneliness was directly associated with SI, whereas its association with low meaning in life was borderline.  Meaning in life may play a relevant role in the psychosocial factors examined and SI, although longitudinal research is needed. Interventions enhancing meaning and addressing loneliness may improve suicide prevention in nursing homes.

records.title: Supporting Diversity in Health and Aging Research and Education: Recommendations from a Multidisciplinary Gerontological Symposium
records.abstract: Increasing attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have left many researchers and educators in aging scrambling on how best to navigate this political landscape in their research and teaching. In response, the Gerontological Society of America (GSA)’s Public Policy Advisory Panel convened a multidisciplinary panel discussion of experts from the six GSA member groups and three advisory panels in November 2025 to discuss the current state of the research and education, particularly as it relates to diversity in health and aging; current efforts by researchers and educators to adapt and respond to these efforts; and future actionable recommendations on how to continue to support DEI principles in all phases of health and aging research and education. Several common themes emerged across disciplines (collaboration, education, mentorship, and research) that led to four key recommendations: (1) cultivate authentic community relationships and collaboration; (2) intentionally engage historically excluded populations; (3) innovate; and (4) invoke national and state professional and competency standards. Ultimately, this multidisciplinary convening and its ensuing recommendations provide gerontological researchers and educators with both context and guidance for navigating recent attacks on DEI and contribute to a broader conversation on this important topic.

records.title: Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families
records.abstract: and  The rise of transnational families has generated new care arrangements in which migrant children use digital technologies to support ageing parents across borders. While the functional role of digital technologies in facilitating remote care is well documented, their relational and culturally embedded dimensions remain less understood. This review synthesises recent evidence on how digital technologies shape transnational caregiving. Research Design and  Eight electronic sources were systematically searched for studies on transnational families, ageing, digital technology (including artificial intelligence—AI), and care, published between 2020 and 2025. Eligible studies were extracted, coded, and analysed using thematic analysis.  Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis. Five themes were identified: 1) adoption and challenges for transnational ICT-mediated care; 2) ambivalence towards digital intimacy; 3) emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care; 4) cultural norms and moral hierarchies of digital care; 5) structural inequalities in transnational care. Digital technologies both foster connection and amplify separation, serving as symbolic markers of family devotion and tools for managing information across generations. Rather than democratising care, technologies often reinforce existing global North–South, gendered, and class-based inequalities.  Digital technologies both sustain and transform transnational care, yet digitally mediated care remains relational and structurally constrained. Stronger digital inclusion and coordinated cross-border care infrastructures are needed to support ageing transnational families, while avoiding the reproduction of existing social, gendered, and global inequalities, and enabling older adults to age with dignity, connection, and security.

records.title: Integrating Perceived Psychosocial Outcomes Into the Assessment of Telecare Acceptability Among Slovenian Informal Caregivers of Older People: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
records.abstract: While telecare has considerable potential to improve home care services, benefit older adults, and support informal caregivers, its adoption remains limited. There is also a notable gap in empirical research on the factors that influence informal caregivers’ behavioral intention to use telecare. In particular, existing theoretical acceptance models are insufficiently comprehensive, as they do not specifically address informal caregivers of older adults and have largely overlooked the psychosocial outcomes of engaging with telecare.  This study examined the behavioral intention of Slovenian informal caregivers of older adults to use telecare, focusing on the preuse stage of technology acceptance, by integrating the perceived psychosocial outcomes of telecare engagement (peace of mind, reduced anxiety, sense of safety, and perceived connectedness with the care recipient) into the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model.  The study applied nested ordinary least squares regression analysis to survey data collected in 2021 in Slovenia from informal caregivers of older adults, all of whom were aged 40 years or older. Of 612 respondents in the dataset, 558 were retained after excluding current or former users of care-related assistive technologies; the regression analyses were based on the 526 participants with complete data on all model variables.  The regression analysis used 3 nested models to examine predictors of the intention of informal caregivers of older adults to use telecare. The first model, which included only  variables (burden of care, financial coping, and caregiver sociodemographic characteristics), had limited explanatory power ( R ²=0.03), with financial coping as the only significant predictor (β=−0.14, P =.005). Adding UTAUT predictors significantly improved the model’s fit ( R ²=0.49). Performance expectancy (β=0.52, P P =.005), and social influence (β=0.21, P R ²=0.54); this additional factor also showed the strongest association (β=0.41, P  In this cross-sectional sample, perceived psychosocial outcomes were the predictors most strongly associated with behavioral intention in the extended UTAUT model, indicating that they may be important factors in understanding telecare acceptability among informal caregivers. The findings suggest that developers, policymakers, and health and social care providers should consider not only functional aspects of telecare but also the psychosocial needs of informal caregivers. As the study measured self-reported intention at the preuse stage rather than actual use, longitudinal and behavioral research is needed to establish whether these associations translate into telecare adoption.

records.title: Multilingual Dementia Training for Paid Caregivers: A RE-AIM Mixed-Methods Evaluation
records.abstract: and  This study evaluated the IHSS+ ADRD Training Project, a multilingual intervention for caregivers serving individuals living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) through California’s In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) program, using the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework. Research Design and  A quasi-experimental, mixed- evaluation was conducted from July 2019 to June 2024 across Alameda and Los Angeles counties. By applying the RE-AIM framework, Reach and Effectiveness dimensions were assessed through surveys completed by 488 caregivers in English (n = 297), Spanish (n = 102), and Chinese (n = 89) at pre-training, post-training, and 3-month follow-up. Caregivers were diverse among English speakers (38% Black/African American, 23% Hispanic/Latino, and 20% Asian), averaged 49.9 years old, and were predominantly women (88%). Quantitative measures assessed dementia knowledge, self-efficacy, distress, and depression. Qualitative interviews with stakeholders (n = 11) and open-ended caregiver survey responses explored Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance dimensions  RE-AIM findings demonstrated: Reach across diverse caregiver populations in multilingual formats; Effectiveness with significant improvements in dementia knowledge and self-efficacy sustained at 3-month follow-up, plus 88-99% satisfaction; Adoption facilitated by union partnership; Implementation successfully transitioned to virtual delivery during COVID-19 despite technology barriers; and Maintenance supported by increased caregiver confidence, self-care awareness, and stress management skills, though sustainability required ongoing funding.  Language-concordant training produced meaningful, sustained improvements across a diverse paid caregiver workforce, demonstrating its value as an equity strategy in home care workforce development. While virtual delivery was feasible and cost-effective, long-term success depends on securing dedicated funding and reliable technology infrastructure.

records.title: Patterns of Social Participation Among Community-Dwelling People With Dementia in Japan: Individual and Neighborhood Correlates
records.abstract: Social participation supports quality of life among people with dementia, yet participation patterns and their correlates remain poorly understood.  To identify patterns of leisure activities, community group participation, and social contact and their individual and neighborhood correlates.  We analyzed cross-sectional data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study–Home Care linked with Long-Term Care Insurance records ( n = 1,604; aged ≥65 years with dementia). Fourteen participation-related indicators were analyzed using latent class analysis. Correlates were examined using bias-adjusted multinomial logistic regression adjusted for sex and age.  Three classes were identified: Broad (10.1%), Relationship-based (21.9%), and Limited (68.0%). Compared with Limited participation, both other classes were associated with younger age, living alone, greater functional independence, lower dementia severity, and more favorable perceived walkability and availability of parks or walking paths.  Findings suggest that participation support should consider individual characteristics and perceived characteristics of the neighborhood physical environment.

records.title: Levels of Digital Engagement Among Older Adults in South Korea: A Latent Profile Analysis and Implications for Digital Inclusion
records.abstract: Digital inequality among older adults involves within-group differences in the levels of digital engagement across multiple everyday-life domains.  This study identified levels of digital engagement among Korean adults aged 65 and older and examined factors associated with profile membership.  Using data from the 2022 Digital Divide Survey, latent profile analysis was conducted, followed by multinomial logistic regression using a manual three-step approach.  Three engagement profiles emerged: low (46.2%), moderate (46.3%), and high engagement (7.5%). Gender, residential area, digital device self-efficacy, and digital attitudes were significantly associated with profile membership, whereas household income was not significantly associated with profile membership. These findings indicate differences in levels of digital engagement among older adults and highlight associations with selected sociodemographic, individual, and contextual factors.

records.title: Providers’ Perspective on Barriers and Solutions to Adult Day Services Provision in Ohio
records.abstract: Adult day services (ADS) are essential home- and community-based supports, yet providers continue to face significant post-COVID operational and engagement challenges. Limited state-level evidence constrains efforts to strengthen ADS capacity.  To identify barriers experienced by ADS providers in Ohio and provider-driven solutions to sustain and strengthen services in the post-COVID environment.  A sequential mixed- design integrated pre-survey focus groups ( n = 17), a statewide provider survey ( n = 28), and post-survey focus groups ( n = 11). Descriptive statistics and thematic analysis were used to synthesize findings.  Two themes emerged: (1) Participants, Family, and Community Engagement, characterized by limited public awareness, caregiver hesitation, and unstable referral pathways; and (2) Operational Challenges and Limited Resources, including financial strain, staffing shortages, transportation barriers, administrative burden, and facility limitations. Providers identified solutions such as statewide education, workforce development, shared transportation models, and regulatory streamlining.

records.title: Longitudinal Association Between Prefrailty/Frailty and HIV-associated Neurocognitive Disorder (HAND): a Mexican Prospective Study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Geriatric syndromes such as frailty may be more prevalent and occur earlier in people aging with HIV, negatively impacting outcomes like cognition. Cross-sectional data show strong associations between pre-frailty/frailty and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND). However, prospective studies suggest baseline HAND increases frailty risk, while pre-frailty/frailty do not predict HAND onset. We aimed to investigate longitudinal association between baseline frailty and HAND category progression. Longitudinal analysis of 194 participants aged ≥50 years from Mexico City referral center. Two standardized geriatric assessments performed at least one year apart. HAND defined using Antinori criteria, frailty by Fried phenotype. Inverse probability weighted Cox models adjusted for confounders from directed acyclic graph (age, educational level, detectable viral load, diabetes, stroke, ischemic heart disease) determined association between frailty and HAND progression. Median age 55 (53–61) years; 167 (86%) men; median follow-up 2.3 (1.6–3.1) years. Baseline: 129 (66.4%) robust, 62 (31.9%) pre-frail, 3 (1.5%) frail. No longitudinal association between pre-frailty/frailty and HAND progression was observed in this cohort (32 progression events; adjusted HR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.27–1.48; p = 0.29). No evidence of a prospective association between prefrailty/frailty and HAND category progression was observed in this cohort; most participants remained cognitively stable. To our knowledge, this is the first study describing HAND trajectories and their relationship with prefrailty/frailty in older adults with HIV in Mexico and Latin America.
